newsitem.title: JAPAN: Big Japanese firms say to stay in Thailand for now.
newsitem.headline: Big Japanese firms say to stay in Thailand for now.

text.p: Thailand's drastic economic reform plans have made some Japanese companies worried about their future business in the country but several major firms said on Wednesday they would not change their operations immediately.
"We will not change our business in Thailand immediately, but we will consider how we can adjust it to Thailand's situation," a spokesman for Toyota Motor Corp said.
Japan's top carmaker would seriously study the situation but it was unlikely to greatly change its operations in view of its long history in Thailand, he said.

Thailand's government on Tuesday unveiled a set of reforms to help ease its economic woes after the baht came under fierce attack from investors worried about the country's excessive foreign borrowing and frail banking system. The baht has lost 20 percent of its value since it was allowed to float on July 2.

The programme is aimed at securing about $15 billion in loans from the International Monetary Fund and foreign nations. It includes the suspension of operations of more than half of Thailand's finance companies, a three percentage point rise in the value-added tax, and strict monetary and fiscal targets for the next few years.

As of the end of April, a total of 1,148 Japanese companies and their units were registered at the Japanese chamber of commerce and industry in Bangkok, up from 424 firms in 1986, the Japan External Trade Organisation said.
An increasing number of Japanese firms have shifted some of their production to Southeast Asia in the last few decades.
Thailand is a favourite location because of its stable political and economic situation backed by an efficient bureaucracy and a Buddhist-based culture, which Japanese feel familiar with.
In the 1990s, the move was accelerated by the yen's appreciation. Southeast Asia became attractive also as a consumer market due to its rapid economic growth.

Machinery maker Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Ltd, electronics appliance maker Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd, and department store operator Sogo Co Ltd also said they would not change operations in Thailand immediately.
Kobe Steel Ltd, which announced last week it was forming a joint venture in Bangkok in September to produce wire rods for car parts, said it would go ahead with the plan.
"The situation is severe but over the medium- and long-term period, we expect the Thai car industry to grow," a Kobe Steel spokesman said.

Household products manufacturer Kao Corp was more worried. It said it was concerned over a possible fall in consumption in Thailand. "Consumption may become slow due to a higher value-added tax and a fall of the baht, and that would affect us most," a Kao spokesman said. The tax will be raised to 10 percent from seven percent on August 16.
He said material costs are expected to rise and the company may have to further cut production costs in Thailand.
A Matsushita spokesman said that if the baht's drop continued it might have to raise sales prices in Thailand. He said the same would be true of other Japanese makers.
"We will not take any measures immediately but we will consider appropriate steps in broad, company-wide restructuring efforts," he said.
Industry analysts said domestic demand in Thailand has already been sluggish for some time and the economic measures would likely further dampen sentiment.
Hisao Matsuura, an analyst at Nikko Research Center, said Japanese companies would consider shifting their business to outside Thailand.
"Japanese companies will think once again what is the merit of doing business in Thailand," Matsuura said, adding that they will have to face a tough decision.

"Bringing production back to Japan (from Thailand) is not a good idea. And they will also face difficulty in deciding which neighbouring Asian nations to move to when they think of factors such as the political situation, infrastructure and climate," he said.
